visible_solution: Read the wanted-wing cards (color and sigil), locate the matching moving wings in the first-person sanctuary, and use the full surface (WASD, canvas drag for look, and canvas click to throw) to choose a useful launch position and camera direction. Aim for the wing's future three-dimensional position, compensating for gravity and obstacles, release a capsule, inspect the flight and contact in later frames, and repeat for each wanted wing without spending the finite ammunition on decoys. Click CERTIFY ROUNDUP after all wanted contacts are secured.

reasoning.visual: The solution must recover horizontal position, height, and depth from a perspective first-person canvas, distinguish the wanted wing appearances from the scene, and route a capsule through visible terraced geometry. The projectile direction is three-dimensional and the contact test uses x, y, and z distance.
reasoning.temporal: Each creature has nonzero x, y, and z motion, and each tick advances the creatures while an in-flight projectile advances under gravity. The agent must use the changing target state to lead a shot and observe the resulting flight/contact; this is not only an automatic transition to a static answer. The same temporal dependency remains in every difficulty profile and both interaction modes.
reasoning.reasoning_planning: Success requires choosing yaw and pitch for a ballistic trajectory from the launch position, accounting for range, height, target motion, and obelisk collisions. At difficulty 4 the agent must sequence three wanted captures, avoid two decoys, and conserve eight capsules; those choices affect later chances. The lower profiles retain the same 3D gravity/contact decision even when they reduce counts or obstacles.
reasoning.exploration_interface: No exploratory interaction is required. The initial visible UI supplies the wanted color/sigil cards, the prompt and rules, the input-surface instructions, the 3-axes-plus-gravity contact model, the clock, and ammunition. The simplified buttons are also explicitly labeled; later frames and routine contact feedback provide task state rather than revealing a hidden rule or teaching an unknown interface. No profile changes this requirement.

source_evidence.claim: The generated world has a first-person player with x/y/z position, terraces and optional 3D obstacles; physics exposes gravity, projectile speed, radius, and tick limits.
The canvas projection computes side, vertical, and depth coordinates from x/y/z relative to yaw and pitch.
The authoritative replay derives a three-axis throw and accepts contact using Euclidean x/y/z distance while checking 3D obstacle intersection.
Creature positions are functions of tick-dependent phase in all three coordinates.
Every step advances creature positions and projectile age/position/vertical velocity, resolves collisions against the current creature state, and runs until capture or exhaustion.
The visible UI says wings keep moving during flight, instructs the agent to lead the moving wing and inspect the next frame, and exposes the changing sanctuary tick.
A throw converts the current camera yaw/pitch and player launch position into a finite-speed projectile and spends ammunition.
The replay advances later state from earlier input, handles obstacle/decoy/miss outcomes, requires all target IDs, and reports the finite capture result at certification.

The initial render displays wanted appearance cues, the prompt, controls, contact model, clock, ammunition, and certification control; it binds either labeled proxy controls or explicitly described full controls immediately.
Both interaction profiles are implemented as explicit surfaces, with simplified one-tick movement/look/throw proxies and a described full keyboard/mouse surface.
